name: David Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I study business administration. Mondays and Tuesdays are accounting and marketing lectures, Wednesday is free, and I use it to catch up with notes, because I like to write everything out and file it properly. On Saturdays I pick parcels at a depot from six in the morning, which is dull but pays fine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad is an electrician with his own small firm and my mum works in the town council's housing office. They pay half of my room in a flat I share with two lads from my course. The rest comes from the depot, about 100 a week, and I try to spend very little. I don't like owing anyone money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so. I've never used any of these tools and I don't plan to, and if they're mostly hype, I've lost nothing. At the depot Karim (a coworker) keeps showing me clips of robots doing things, and I'd just say let's see it in the real warehouse first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel settled. My degree leads to jobs in banks, insurers and firms, and those have been there for decades. I'd still worry a bit about the graduate market being tough, because plenty of people have business degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now: study, work Saturdays, save about 30 a week. I'd apply for a placement year at an insurer in third year, which is the normal route. I wouldn't change anything, because there's nothing to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a normal year in a normal world. My own worry is more about rent and a first job, which are always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lads in the flat who do use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it feels like a good bet, with the usual risk. Plenty of my course will compete for the same placements. But a business degree is practical, and I'd say that in a world without big change it's a safe path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the degree still feel like a good bet to you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them, use whatever you like, but I'll keep writing everything out. If anything breaks, you'll know where to find me with a pen. It's a joke, but it's also true.

say: I'd tell the lads in the flat that I never needed the tools, **told you so**.
At the depot I'd tell Karim to show me robots working in the **real** warehouse first.
think: My business degree leads to banks, insurers and firms that have hired for **decades**.
The graduate market is still tough, with many people competing for the same **placements**.
do: Keep studying and picking parcels, saving about **30 a week**.
Apply for a **placement year** at an insurer in third year.
feel: **Calm**, like a normal year in a normal world, with only the usual worry about rent.
S0.quote: My degree leads to jobs in banks, insurers and firms, and those have been there for decades.
fieldNote: He is calm because the world looks **familiar** and the path is the usual one.
He jokes about writing everything out, which shows he's comfortable being the traditional one in the flat.
His real worry is rent and a first job, not AI.

steps.text: Keep picking parcels at the depot every Saturday
Save 30 a week into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see how it goes. I'd tell my dad that businesses still need people they can trust, and I'd say the same to my course mates. I wouldn't post anything online, I don't have much to say about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's a real threat to what I'm studying. A lot of business work is checking figures, writing reports, and booking things, and those tasks sit right where software is strong. If firms hire fewer juniors, I'm in the group that gets squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the degree going, and I'd start to learn a bit of how the tools are used in banks and insurance, from a safe distance. I'd take an evening course in basic spreadsheets and data. I'd cut my spending and save 50 a week, because I'd want a cushion before the graduate market tightens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not the sort of fear that keeps me up, but it sits there when I look at the course list and wonder which parts are worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a business degree job would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Accounting checks, filling in forms, and drafting standard letters. Those were the jobs I thought I'd start in. If a program does them in seconds, my first job would be harder to get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your course friends all started using it and you didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel stubborn about it, to be honest. I'd probably hold off until I could see that employers actually value these skills. But I'd be nervous that waiting means I fall behind, so I might give in and take the spreadsheet course first.

say: I'd tell my dad that firms still need people they can **trust**.
I wouldn't post anything online, because I don't have much to **say**.
think: Checking figures, writing reports and booking things sit right where software is **strong**.
If firms hire fewer **juniors**, I'm in the group that gets squeezed.
do: Take an evening course in **spreadsheets** and data, from a safe distance.
Cut spending and save **50 a week** for a cushion.
feel: **Anxious** in a quiet way, wondering which parts of the course are worth it.
S1.quote: Accounting checks, filling in forms, and drafting standard letters. Those were the jobs I thought I'd start in.
fieldNote: He names the **junior tasks** he hoped to start in and sees them at risk.
His resistance is real, but he admits waiting may leave him behind.
He doesn't talk online about it, which fits his private style.

steps.text: Take an evening course in spreadsheets and data basics
Cut takeaway meals and nights out to save more
Save 50 a week for a cushion before the market tightens
Wait to see which skills employers ask for before buying courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, I don't know. Everybody will be saying something different, and I'd keep quiet until I could work out what's true. I'd talk to my parents and a few course mates, but I wouldn't announce anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel very worried. If AI does almost any thinking job better and cheaper, a business degree is exactly what would lose value. I'd also worry that my parents' jobs, my mum's council office work, would be affected too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents what savings we have, and I'd work more Saturdays at the depot, because hands-on work lasts longer. I'd talk to my dad about joining his firm as an apprentice electrician over the summer, to have a second path. I'd also cut all my spending to the bare minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the safe path I picked has suddenly turned into a trap, and I don't like surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years do to the plans you've made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His firm is safer for a while because wiring a house needs hands, and robots are later. But his paperwork, quotes and scheduling would change on day one. I'd say he should keep a good cash reserve and I'd help with the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about his firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would flip my plans upside down. I'd go from placement-year-at-an-insurer to maybe learning a trade. It's not what I imagined, but it's real work. I'd rather have a skill that holds up than a degree that doesn't.

say: I'd keep quiet until I could work out what's **true**.
I'd talk to my parents and a few course mates but not **announce** anything.
think: A business degree is exactly what would **lose value** if AI does thinking jobs better and cheaper.
My mum's council **office** work could be affected too.
do: Work **more Saturdays** at the depot and cut all spending to the minimum.
Ask my dad about an **apprentice** electrician role as a second path.
feel: **Alarmed**, as though the safe path I chose has turned into a trap.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a skill that holds up than a degree that doesn't.
fieldNote: The safe business degree turns into a **liability** in his mind.
He turns to his father's trade as a second path, because robots come later for hands-on work.
He tends to go quiet and ask family, not announce views.

steps.text: Cut every non-essential cost and work extra Saturdays at the depot
Ask my parents to open a joint emergency savings account
Start a summer apprenticeship under my dad's electrician firm
Help my dad with his quotes and books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but we have a bit of time. I'd keep my views mostly private and talk with my parents about what we'd do. I'd probably say to my mates that they should have a second plan, in case the degree isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still worried, but I'm not scared out of my mind. I'd graduate in 2029, which gives me maybe two working years before things change a lot. That's not a lot, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, because it's three more years and a lot of money already spent. I'd add a trade certificate in electrical basics or building maintenance, through my dad's contacts, in my summers. I'd keep saving 50 a week and avoid any debt that isn't loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a long, slow worry rather than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time lets me do two things at once: finish and prepare. With two years I'd have to drop everything. With five I can do both slowly, which is how I like to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still finish the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish it, yes. I'd say it's a degree, a proof I can finish something, and a social network. It doesn't have to be my whole plan.

say: I'd tell my mates to have a **second plan** in case the degree isn't enough.
I'd keep most of my views **private** and talk with my parents.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with maybe two **working years** before things change a lot.
Five years lets me finish and **prepare** at the same time.
do: Finish the degree because the money is already **spent**.
Add a trade **certificate** through my dad's contacts over the summers.
feel: **Anxious** in a long, slow way, not panic.
S3.quote: With two years I'd have to drop everything. With five I can do both slowly, which is how I like to do things.
fieldNote: He likes doing things **slowly**, and five years fits that temperament.
He plans a second skill but keeps the degree as proof he can finish something.
He avoids debt other than the loan, which matches his general caution.

steps.text: Finish the business degree with a placement year
Do a summer building maintenance certificate through my dad's contacts
Save 50 a week and take no new debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see. Ten years is long, and plenty of things people said would happen didn't. I'd keep an open mind and say we should keep watching but not freak out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly settled. I'd be 28, with a job and a few years of experience, and I'd have time to adapt without being forced. I'd still worry about my parents' retirement and whether pensions stay safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a placement, and take the first graduate job I can. I'd save 60 a week once I'm earning and put some into a safe fund. I'd probably try the AI tools once they've been around long enough that everyone's using them and they've been checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only slightly. It's like hearing about a big storm that's still far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: would it change what you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pick something you'd be happy doing, not what looks safe. And learn to work with people, because I think that's what's left. Don't just chase the highest salary, which is advice I'm still trying to learn myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin who's choosing a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep my degree choice the same. A decade is long enough for the degree to matter. What would change is how I work in the job. I'd use the tools like everyone else once they're proven, and not before.

say: I'd say plenty of things people predicted **didn't** happen, so let's keep watching.
I'd tell friends not to **freak out**.
think: I'd be 28 with a job and time to **adapt** without being forced.
I'd still worry about my parents' **pensions** staying safe.
do: Finish the degree, take a placement and the first graduate **job** I can.
Save 60 a week once earning and use AI tools when they're **proven**.
feel: **Uneasy** but only slightly, like a storm far away.
S4.quote: I'd say pick something you'd be happy doing, not what looks safe. And learn to work with people, because I think that's what's left.
fieldNote: With a decade he is only **slightly** uneasy, and his worry moves to his parents' pensions.
He is willing to use AI later, once others have proven it, which matches his resistant profile.
He admits he struggles to follow his own advice about chasing salary.

steps.text: Finish the degree and take a placement year
Save 60 a week once I have a first salary
Try AI tools at work once colleagues use them daily

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years isn't enough for a plain person to work out what to do, and everyone around me would be guessing at the same time. What would help is clear information from somewhere I trust, and some kind of guaranteed support so people aren't left to cope alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I don't think so. I'd just say that I'm not against new things, I just want to see them work first. I'd rather be second and sure than first and wrong.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things, I just want to see them work first. I'd rather be second and sure than first and wrong.
portrait: David is 18 and studies **business administration**, with top school results and a flat share his parents help pay for.
He picks parcels on Saturdays, spends little, hates owing money and **never uses AI tools**.
He is a centrist who wants to see things proven first, blames nobody in particular and trusts **clear information**.
His mood moves from calm to alarmed as warning time shrinks, because office jobs and his **dad's** firm both feel exposed.
He tends to keep going and save, and to wait and watch before acting.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, because two years is too little for ordinary people to work out what to do.
whatWouldHelp: He wants clear, **trusted information** and guaranteed support, so people aren't left to cope alone.
